channel.title: TapeReader Research Notes
channel.description: Dated research notes on markets: how drops unfold, how well-known investors actually work, and what holds up in the data.

item.title: From $500 to $1 million in ten trading days: a Reddit options run, read off NVDA's chart
item.description: A Reddit account went from about $2,600 to $1,021,075 between 11 and 25 November 2026 by buying cheap, short-dated NVDA options with a fifth to a half of the account each time; four overnight gaps produced 81% of the profit shown, and the last position was worth $740,000 at 9:32 am and $95,000 by the close.

item.title: Options for someone who trades stocks: a primer
item.description: An option is a rented, expiring, leveraged position in a stock; the huge gains in screenshots come from buying cheap options that expire soon, in size, just before a move larger than the market had priced in, and the same recipe loses the whole stake on most other days.

item.title: Making room for luck: a reading of the Luck Field Manual, with the evidence checked
item.description: A popular 33-rule guide says luck can be engineered; its ideas reduce to three jobs (meet more chances, survive the bad ones, notice the good ones), the research behind them is strong for some rules and thin for others, and the advice only works where a failed attempt is cheap.

item.title: Hedge funds, concentrated bets and short selling: a primer on big positions, public pressure and the cost of being early
item.description: A hedge fund is a private partnership that may borrow, sell short and put most of its money into a few positions, and the record shows that these freedoms produced a handful of famous results while the average fund, after fees, trailed both a plain index fund and a 60/40 portfolio over the last ten and twenty years.

item.title: Bill Ackman: ten positions and capital that cannot leave
item.description: Ackman's audited record is about 16% a year since 2004 from roughly ten large positions and a few cheap hedges, but it includes four losing years in a row, and the listed fund has trailed the S&P 500 since its own launch in 2012.

item.title: Michael Burry: the price of being early
item.description: Burry's one documented record (2000 to mid-2008, about 26% a year after fees, known from investor letters) came from reading documents nobody else read and from bets whose loss was capped at a premium; since 2008 no returns have been published, and his public market warnings since 2019 were followed by a higher index far more often than by a lower one.

item.title: Investor styles: 30 names, one set of questions
item.description: The plan for a series on how 30 well-known investors actually invest, the 14 questions every profile answers, and how the records will be graded and ranked.

item.title: Global macro: a primer on trading currencies, interest rates and whole markets
item.description: Global macro traders bet on whole economies with borrowed money, and the part of their method that an individual can use is the free public data they watch to decide how much risk to carry.

item.title: Stan Druckenmiller: big bets, small losses
item.description: Druckenmiller's results came less from being right than from betting large in liquid markets when conviction was high, cutting fast when wrong, and standing aside when cold; the famous 30% a year rests on press reports of his own firm's numbers, not on a public audited series.

item.title: Ray Dalio: rules, many small bets, and a record in two halves
item.description: Ray Dalio built the largest hedge fund by writing his decisions down as testable rules and spreading risk over many unrelated bets, and the record shows the method worked very well until 2011, poorly from 2012 to 2024, and well again once the fund shrank.

item.title: Value investing: a primer on buying businesses for less than they are worth
item.description: Value investing means buying a share of a business for well below a careful estimate of its worth, and the record shows the idea is sound while cheap stocks lagged for most of 2007 to 2025 and most stock pickers trail an index.

item.title: Warren Buffett: patience, float and a record that changed after 1998
item.description: Buffett's 19.7% a year over 61 years is the best-documented record in investing, but it rests on cheap insurance money and permanent capital as much as on stock picking, nearly all of the lead over the index was built before 1999, and what an individual can take from it is the behaviour, not the structure.

item.title: Peter Lynch: a category for every stock
item.description: Lynch's 29.2% a year at Magellan is real and well documented, but two-thirds of its margin over the index came in four early years when the fund was tiny and closed to the public; what lasts is the habit of deciding what kind of position a stock is before buying it, because the kind sets what to expect and when to sell.

item.title: Quantitative and multi-strategy investing: a primer on small edges, many bets and tight risk limits
item.description: Quantitative investing turns a small tested edge into a return by repeating it many thousands of times with borrowed money and strict loss limits, and the record shows that most edges found in old data shrink once they are traded and that the average quant product has trailed a plain index fund.

item.title: Jim Simons: a small edge, repeated millions of times
item.description: Medallion's reported 66% a year before fees is not in audited public filings but is corroborated by a Senate report and by the firm's own statements to a US regulator; it came from being right slightly more than half the time on millions of small, short, heavily borrowed trades in a fund capped near $10bn and closed to outsiders, and the funds Renaissance sold to the public did not repeat it.

item.title: Ken Griffin: the firm is the edge
item.description: Griffin's record comes from an organisation, not from one trader's calls: hundreds of hedged books under central risk control, financed with heavy leverage and locked-up capital, with costs charged to investors; the one year the financing failed, 2008, the funds lost 55%.

item.title: Anatomy of a drop: how market falls unfold and end
item.description: A 24-page study of US stock-market drops since 1950, built around the comparison of autumn 2026 with autumn 2018, and with 2000 and 2007 as the other path.

item.title: AI Buildout Atlas: where the money goes, in the West and in China
item.description: A 32-page atlas of the AI build-out in ten layers, from the power grid to the apps people pay for, mapped once for the West and once for China on the same definitions.
